analysis.one_liner: Requires pollution standards to protect children with extra safety margins and bans toxic pesticides in schools.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, vote, or a single cosponsor and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee at the end of 2002.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Barbara Boxer's bill would have rewritten how the EPA sets pollution limits so that children, pregnant women, the elderly, and the chronically ill get an extra margin of safety. Where scientists lacked data on how a pollutant affects children, agencies would have had to assume it is more dangerous to them and tighten the standard by at least a factor of ten. Schools and day care centers would have had to stop using pesticides linked to cancer, nerve damage, or hormone disruption, notify parents before any spraying, and post warning signs. It also would have forced companies to report more of their releases of chemicals like lead, mercury, and dioxin, and given families plain-language guides to reducing children's exposure.
analysis.who_benefits: Children would gain the most: pollution standards would have to account for their greater susceptibility, hazardous pesticides would be barred from schools and day care centers, and parents would get 72-hour notice and posted signs before any spraying. Pregnant women, the elderly, and the chronically ill would be covered by the same safety margins. Families would get plain-language guides to safer products and exposure reduction, and communities would learn more about local releases of chemicals like lead, mercury, and dioxin through expanded reporting requirements.

how_it_helps.text: Directed EPA to make every pollution standard protect children and other vulnerable groups with an adequate margin of safety, and to add an extra 10-fold safety margin wherever data on children's susceptibility were missing.

Banned schools and day care centers receiving federal funds from applying pesticides containing known or probable carcinogens, developmental or reproductive toxins, acute nerve toxins, or endocrine disrupters, with a 14-day emergency exemption.
Required schools and day care centers to give parents written notice 72 hours before any pesticide application and to post warning signs during application.
Directed EPA to publish lists of pollutants found where children are present, safer alternative products, and a family right-to-know information kit on reducing children's exposure.

Expanded the Toxics Release Inventory so facilities would have to report releases of chemicals that persist, bioaccumulate, or disrupt endocrine systems — specifically including lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, and chromium — at thresholds capturing at least 80 percent of aggregate releases.

Created a Children's Environmental Health Protection Advisory Committee of pediatricians, educators, and community and public health representatives to flag standards that need reevaluation, and directed federal agencies to research how pollutants affect children.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical and pesticide manufacturers would bear the main costs: tighter pollution standards with built-in child safety margins, a loss of the school pesticide market for products with carcinogens, nerve toxins, or endocrine disrupters, and expanded reporting of toxic releases. Schools and day care centers would face pest-control changes, notice duties, and warning-sign requirements, though the bill authorized federal funds to help.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed real compliance costs on schools and day care centers: a mandatory shift toward least-toxic pest control, written parental notice 72 hours before every pesticide application, and posted warning signs, all without dedicated funding beyond a catch-all authorization of appropriations.

It presumed harm where science was unsettled, requiring EPA to apply an added margin of safety of at least 10-fold whenever data on children's susceptibility were lacking — a conservative default that could tighten standards faster than the underlying evidence justified.

The annual requirement to re-propose at least three existing standards risked turning major rulemaking into a routine quota, which critics of the approach said could produce rushed or formulaic regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were broad and concrete: tighter safety margins for the people most exposed to pollution, an end to spraying known carcinogens and nerve toxins where children learn and play, advance warning for parents, and more public reporting on toxic releases. The costs were real but narrow: schools and day care centers would have had to change pest-control practices and send notices, and chemical and pesticide makers would have faced tighter standards and more disclosure, with some costs likely passed on. The bill included escape valves — a 14-day emergency exemption from the school pesticide ban and an EPA process to publish reasons for declining to revise any standard — which blunts the objection that it was too rigid. On balance it was a modest-cost, broad-benefit bill, and its biggest design weakness was political: it was introduced with no cosponsors and no committee work behind it, so it never got the chance to prove itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Barbara Boxer introduced the Children's Environmental Protection Act in the Senate on May 9, 2001.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never reported the bill back to the Senate, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

If enacted, it would have amended the Toxic Substances Control Act to require child-protective safety margins in EPA standards, banned hazardous pesticides in federally funded schools and day care centers, and expanded toxic release reporting for chemicals like lead, mercury, and dioxin.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide and chemical manufacturers were better off: they faced no new school-use bans, no added child safety margins in pollution standards, and no expanded toxic release reporting. Children and parents got none of the promised protections.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 9, 2001 and never held a markup or reported it back to the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and not a single senator — from either party — cosponsored it, so its partisan support was never tested.

industries.note: The bill barred federally funded schools and day care centers from applying pesticides containing carcinogens, nerve toxins, or endocrine disrupters and forced advance parental notice for any spraying, shrinking a school market and raising scrutiny of products. Industry's interest ran against the bill's child-safety purpose. Sources: S2, S3

Expanded toxic release reporting for bioaccumulative and endocrine-disrupting chemicals — lead, mercury, dioxin, cadmium, chromium — would have forced many facilities to measure and disclose emissions and pressured tighter pollution standards. Cheaper disposal and secrecy about releases are what the bill took away. Sources: S2, S3

The bill saddled them with notice requirements, posted signs, and a shift to least-toxic pest control, but gave them a federal playbook, safer-product lists, and emergency flexibility. Children and parents got the safer side of that trade. Sources: S2, S3
